hn.title: Drawgent: Coding agent on a live Excalidraw canvas

product.launch_state: 0.2.1 released 2026-09-29; repo README updated 2026-09-29; docs/extension touched 2026-09-28-30. Young, single-author, HN-front-page project.

what_it_is: Not an MCP server you wire into a chat client, and not a one-shot prompt-to-image generator: drawgent is a local server that puts YOUR already-installed coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, or opencode) on a live, persistent Excalidraw canvas that a human and the agent edit together.

It never ships an agent. It drives your install, your login, your config and your repository: `drawgent setup claude` then `drawgent up` in a repo. No Node.js and no Docker are required, unlike most of the field.

Two-way loop: the agent reads the canvas (`get_scene` incrementally, `get_screenshot` cropped PNG, `check_layout` geometry lint with no screenshot at all) and writes to it (add_graph auto-layout, add_mermaid, add_elements, update_elements, make_space, delete_elements with an arrow-bridging reconnect, undo_changes).

The differentiator versus every Excalidraw/whiteboard MCP competitor: diagrams are linked to CODE. A shape can point at a file, a line range and a symbol; link status is checked as ok/moved/stale/missing and `drawgent check` fails CI when they break. 'Build what I drew' turns diagram edits into implementation work, with planned/in-progress/done/blocked markers drawn on the canvas.

Interaction is spatial, not just typed: a laser gesture (circle, cross-out, arrow A→B, line, ✓, tap, ↔/↕) is recognised along with what it is drawn over, and 2 s later the agent offers 2-3 concrete tasks plus 'Other…'. An `AGENT: …` note written on the canvas fires once typing settles (default 2500 ms) and the agent answers with a green `DONE:` note.

Collaboration: it can join an excalidraw.com room or a self-hosted Excalidraw document as a named collaborator (default '🤖 Agent') via its own WebSocket relay; a Firefox MV3 extension adds a drawgent sidebar to the document you already have open, so laser strokes there become gestures.

Durability: boards can be committed as clean, diffable `.excalidraw` files (`--diagram docs/architecture.excalidraw`), so the diagram follows `git pull` and can be CI-checked. Agent edits sit on the normal undo stack (Ctrl+Z per edit, one control to revert a whole turn).

competitors.name: mcp_excalidraw (agent skill + 26-tool MCP server)
competitors.meta: 2,490 stars, 279 forks, TypeScript, MIT; created 2025-03-16, last push 2026-09-08

Its README draws the line itself: official Excalidraw MCP = 'prompt in, diagram out (one-shot widget)'; this project = 'programmatic element-level control (CLI + 26 MCP tools)'.

angles: The interface bet: chat is a lossy serialisation of a graph. Drawgent's argument is that a diagram does not erase the shape of the problem — you stop describing three services and arrows in prose and hoping the model rebuilds the same graph. This is the most transferable idea in the project and is worth a section on its own.

What makes it NOT just another Excalidraw MCP: code links. A box points at file+lines+symbol; status is ok/moved/stale/missing; `drawgent check` fails CI when architecture documentation drifts. That reframes the diagram from a picture into a testable artifact — the single least-copied feature in the whole comparison set.

The bidirectional trap (strongest counter-argument, already made publicly by a reviewer): a visual interface makes the agent's confidence MORE legible, not more correct. A clean diagram of what it plans to do looks like understanding; it is the same guess a chat reply would have made, rendered in boxes that feel authoritative because you draw boxes like that yourself. The canvas is a better place to catch a mistake AND a better place to be fooled by one.

Intent ambiguity is genuinely worse in a picture than in a sentence: one box with an arrow to another could mean 'A calls B', 'A depends on B', 'A becomes B', or 'these are related, figure it out'. A wrong commitment on a fuzzy diagram is worse than a wrong commitment on a fuzzy sentence, because you believed the picture was unambiguous.

Why do agents need a canvas at all when Mermaid exists? The thread's most common answer — several practitioners report Mermaid is the most agent-friendly medium today, and one built an Obsidian plugin around it. Drawgent's counter is human-side: Mermaid cannot be edited by hand in a room, cannot carry a laser gesture, and cannot hold a code link on a shape.

Model training bias as the real technical constraint: 'agents are heavily trained on specific formats (e.g. SVG) and are conversely pretty bad at niche formats' — one commenter built a native renderer so the agent could iterate visually on SVG/PNG output instead of one-shotting a niche format. Relevant to the question of whether Excalidraw JSON is a good agent substrate at all.

Spatial reasoning is where these tools break, and the thread agrees: commenters note the models 'had to deal with a lot of JSON data and estimating/computing with bounding box and pixel point numbers'. Reladraw answers this with a declarative placement language; drawgent answers it with `check_layout` (geometry lint without a screenshot) plus `make_space` and auto-layout graphs. Compare the two answers.

The 'AI slop' backlash is inseparable from this product category: one subthread argues a big part of the appeal of Excalidraw output is that people still think it is hand-made, so connecting an agent to Excalidraw is 'attention arbitrage' — with the blunt reply 'I found a new way of wasting people's time with my slop… god this is bleak.' Any honest review of drawgent has to handle this, because the hand-drawn aesthetic is doing rhetorical work.

The counter-thesis, from the same thread: 'the value I get from producing a diagram is derived from the thinking.' If the agent draws it for you, you may have skipped the understanding you were actually after. Drawgent's own answer is the drill-down/trace/laser loop — it is built for interrogating a diagram, not just generating one.

Distribution versus depth: drawgent is 12 stars and a single static binary; whiteboard-mcp is npx + a free trial and mcp_excalidraw is 2,490 stars. The review angle is whether local-binary, agent-agnostic depth (no Node.js, no Docker, your login) is a durable advantage or just a smaller addressable market.

The honest status read: v0.2.1, launched 4 days before this brief, with an untested macOS build, an untested Codex live attach, rooms that silently wait forever on private documents, and Chrome as a hard dependency. This is a promising alpha with a real idea, not a product — and the docs admit all of it, which is itself a signal of quality.

The 'understand a codebase' onboarding ritual is the most concrete, demonstrable use case: clone an unknown repo, `drawgent up`, 'Map repo' treemap sized by line count, then laser-circle a box for a drill-down into its internals, then laser-arrow A→B to trace the real call/queue/HTTP path. That is a repeatable walkthrough a review can reproduce.

The hand-drawn illusion is a positioning problem, not just an aesthetic one: the sharpest subthread on the launch argues that Excalidraw's value in an agent workflow is partly that readers still believe it is hand-made, and one commenter describes the practice bluntly as attention arbitrage — earning engagement from people with an LLM-negative bias by making generated output look human. The reply it drew ('I found a new way of wasting people's time with my slop… god this is bleak') is the ethical counterweight. A review of drawgent that ignores this reads as naive about what the Excalidraw aesthetic is for.

Star count is the wrong adoption metric in this niche and the review should say so with evidence: 4,907 stars on a skill that has never had a second commit, 5,427 on a first-party MCP untouched since March, versus drawgent's 12 on a repo with 50 commits in three days. Distribution here is measured in commits and HN threads, not stars.

The first-party squeeze is the strategic story: Excalidraw+ moved MCP behind an API key in public beta and hinted the open-source and Plus efforts may merge. drawgent's durable edge is not the canvas — it is code links, CI checking and laser gestures, i.e. exactly the features an API-key SaaS is least likely to copy.

outline: H2: What drawgent actually is (a local server that puts YOUR agent on a live Excalidraw canvas — not another MCP prompt-to-diagram widget)
H2: The 60-second setup: `drawgent setup claude` then `drawgent up` (local binary, no Node.js, no Docker, one Chrome dependency)
H2: The feature that nothing else ships — diagrams linked to code (file + line range + symbol, ok/moved/stale/missing, `drawgent check` in CI)
H2: Point instead of describing: laser gestures, the 2-second task poll, `AGENT:` notes and the `DONE:` reply
H2: Draw → look → adjust: get_scene, get_screenshot and check_layout, and why geometry lint without a screenshot matters for small models
H2: 'Build what I drew' — turning canvas edits into code, with planned/in-progress/done/blocked markers on the drawing
H2: Rooms, the Firefox extension, and working inside a teammate's document (plus the four documented room limits)

H2: How it compares: official Excalidraw MCP (5.4k stars but one-shot and untouched since March), mcp_excalidraw (2.4k stars, 26 tools, no code links), Whiteboard MCP (npx + free trial, prompt-to-diagram), Reladraw (the opposite paradigm) and tldraw
H2: The hard problems nobody has solved: is a sketch unambiguous enough to act on, and does drawing back look like understanding without being it
H2: Where drawgent stands today — v0.2.1, 12 stars, GPL-3.0, untested macOS and Codex attach, and what to watch next
H2: Verdict: who should run drawgent today, and who should wait

H2: FAQ (is drawgent free, does it need an API key, does it work with Claude Code / Codex / opencode, can it keep my architecture diagram from drifting, does it work with excalidraw.com rooms, is it a replacement for Mermaid)

faq.a: Yes — GPL-3.0-or-later, no warranty, no account and no service; you download a single static binary. You still pay for your own agent (Claude Code, Codex or opencode), which drawgent drives rather than ships.

faq.q: Does drawgent need an API key?
faq.a: No key of its own. It uses your existing agent CLI and your existing login. It is the agent-agnostic counterpart to tools that make you bring a provider key.

faq.q: Which coding agents does it work with?
faq.a: Claude Code and Codex through bridges built into drawgent, opencode natively over ACP, and any other ACP-speaking agent via `drawgent serve --agent mine='my-acp-agent --stdio'`.

faq.q: Can it stop my architecture documentation drifting?
faq.a: That is the feature set it is most alone in: shapes link to a file, line range and symbol, the Code tab reports ok/moved/stale/missing, `drawgent check --fix` repairs moved symbols, and the same command is meant to be run in CI so a broken link fails the build.

faq.q: Does it work with a shared excalidraw.com room?
faq.a: Yes, drawgent joins as one more collaborator (default name '🤖 Agent'), but only if the document has a live collaboration room — a private document often has none, in which case drawgent waits indefinitely rather than erroring. Images are not synced.

faq.q: Is it a replacement for Mermaid?
faq.a: No. It can draw Mermaid (add_mermaid supports flowchart, sequence and class diagrams), but its pitch is that a diagram should be a live, hand-editable, code-linked surface instead of a text block that renders once.
No. It is v0.2.1, launched 2026-09-26, 12 stars, with an untested macOS build and an untested Codex live attach, and it hard-depends on Chrome/Chromium as the renderer. Treat it as a promising alpha.
